However, as the range of possible initial and target configurations grows, goal-conditioned deformable manipulation requires a robot to infer increasingly diverse manipulation behaviors in addition to precise continuous actions. We introduce DefFlow, a framework for goal-conditioned manipulation of deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations. DefFlow learns from demonstrations by jointly predicting the goal-conditioned 3D point flow of the robot and deformable object. We show that this formulation better captures both the manipulation decisions, such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp, and the precise continuous motions required for goal reaching, rather than predicting only the robot flow. Across rope, granular-media, and cloth manipulation settings with diverse initial and target configurations, DefFlow substantially outperforms goal-conditioned action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines on success rates and goal-distance metrics. We further demonstrate deployment of our framework on a real robot using real point-cloud observations and unseen goal configurations.
authors: Gaurav Singh, Sergio Orozco, Ryan Duong, Mete Tuluhan Akbulut, George Konidaris, Srinath Sridhar
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing varied manipulation behaviors and precise motions for deformable objects.
Learns goal-conditioned 3D point flows for both the robot and deformable object from demonstrations.
Captures decisions such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp alongside continuous motion.
Outperforms action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines across rope, granular-media, and cloth settings.
Demonstrates real-robot deployment using point-cloud observations and unseen goal configurations.
papers.selection_reason: Demonstration-based goal-conditioned deformable object manipulation with 3D point flow prediction.
papers.title: DefFlow: Goal-Conditioned Deformable Object Manipulation using 3D Point Flows
papers.tldr: DefFlow enables robots to manipulate deformable objects toward diverse 3D goals by jointly predicting robot and object point flows.

papers.abstract: Blindness and low vision limit many people's ability to complete daily tasks, motivating AI assistants that provide useful guidance. Yet, existing benchmarks do not adequately test whether vision models can provide effective everyday assistance. In particular, i) existing benchmarks primarily rely on visual and textual inputs, with limited support for other modalities that are increasingly available in egocentric wearable devices such as gaze, inertial measurements, spatial trajectories, and others; and ii) existing evaluations emphasize scene understanding and question answering, with limited coverage of goal-conditioned guidance for blind and low-vision users across everyday tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce VISTA (Visually Impaired Scene and Task Annotations), a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal-oriented assistance for blind and low-vision users. VISTA contains $\sim$1,000 egocentric recordings captured with Project Aria glasses; each recording provides synchronized sensor streams, six of which serve as model inputs, and three different types of annotation, covering ten task categories (TC), from object localization to hazard detection. We evaluate 14 representative vision-language models zero-shot on VISTA and design a lightweight multimodal model baseline that integrates all six modalities. Experimental results show that, although existing models can often describe egocentric scenes, they remain limited in generating goal-directed assistive guidance. VISTA thus provides a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models that could improve everyday accessibility.
authors: No\'e Mosca, Mohamed Rayan Barhdadi, Muhammad Hamza, Joshua Yeh, Suryodaya Bikram Shahi, Zhiyan Li, Selim-Antoine Lali, Weiyue Li, Hasan Kurban, Erchin Serpedin, Gang Luo, Yue Zhang, Minghan Li, Mengyu Wang
bullets: Addresses gaps in benchmarks that lack wearable sensor modalities and goal-conditioned assistive guidance.
Includes ~1,000 Project Aria egocentric recordings with synchronized streams, six model-input modalities, and three annotation types.
Covers ten task categories, including object localization and hazard detection.
Evaluates 14 vision-language models zero-shot and introduces a lightweight baseline integrating all six modalities.
Finds that existing models can describe scenes but remain limited in producing effective goal-directed guidance.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VISTA, a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal-oriented assistance, directly relevant to Embodied AI and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: VISTA: A Multimodal Egocentric Benchmark for Goal-Oriented Perception and Assistance to Blind and Low-Vision Users
papers.tldr: VISTA is a multimodal egocentric benchmark for evaluating AI-generated, goal-directed assistance to blind and low-vision users in everyday tasks.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive language models generate text sequentially, but revision requires referring back to tokens in the input context or those already generated. Causal Edit Serialization (CES) is introduced as a framework for expressing such revisions within the same causal token stream. Special pointer tokens are paired with predicted source addresses, allowing insertion, deletion, replacement, copying and movement to be localized explicitly. A lightweight localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding support both address prediction and conditioning on previously emitted pointers, while retaining a standard causal attention mask. A pretraining procedure combines ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model-generated edits and repeated text. Across model scales and editing baselines, CES models demonstrate complete applied edits with modestly higher clean-text bits per byte than clean autoregressive models. Supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training provide a grammatical-error-correction proof of concept, producing more beneficial than harmful changes under reference-blind model judging. Correct repair programs also improve subsequent text prediction while the original context and its cached states are retained. CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer-addressed transformations.
authors: Louis Robinson
bullets: Supports insertion, deletion, replacement, copying, and movement through explicit source-address pointers.
Uses a localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding while preserving standard causal attention.
Pretraining combines language modeling with repairs from random corruptions, generated edits, and repeated text.
Across scales and baselines, models complete edits with only modestly worse clean-text bits per byte than standard models.
A grammatical-error-correction proof of concept shows more beneficial than harmful edits, and correct repairs improve later prediction while cached context is retained.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces causal edit serialization with pointer tokens for autoregressive language models; a novel architecture and training contribution to language foundation models.
papers.title: Causal Edit Serialization
papers.tldr: Causal Edit Serialization lets autoregressive language models perform localized text revisions by encoding edits as pointer-addressed operations in the causal token stream.

papers.abstract: Reliable vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires not only understanding instructions but also determining whether and how a robot can physically execute them. However, existing VLN benchmarks typically assume executable instructions and focus on long-horizon tasks. This leaves body-dependent local execution, including passability and collision-free execution, largely unexamined. Evaluating these factors within long-horizon tasks would entangle local physical execution with task planning and long-term spatial memory, making navigation failures difficult to attribute. We therefore focus on grounding local navigation commands in executable motion under environmental and robot body constraints. We present PASS-VLN, a passability-aware local-command VLN benchmark and model. The benchmark holds the scene, instruction, start pose, and reference route fixed while varying robot body width, requiring target completion when the instructed passage is feasible and stopping before blockage otherwise. Our model encodes body width through obstacle inflation in a depth-derived local bird's-eye view, fuses geometry with visual and linguistic context, and predicts discrete latent action codes for continuous closed-loop execution. Experiments show that PASS-VLN improves collision-free success by approximately 12 percentage points over a strong VLN model fine-tuned on our benchmark, while adapting reach-versus-stop behavior to body constraints and generalizing to unseen body widths. When integrated with a high-level planner, PASS-VLN achieves higher success with fewer local commands, while real-world deployment further demonstrates its effectiveness as a low-level executor. The benchmark and model will be released.
authors: Cong Zou, Xiangsheng Shi, Xuanhui Wang, Fubin Wang, Guangjun Ge, Chao Wang, Yu Wang
bullets: Targets the underexplored problem of body-dependent, collision-free local execution in VLN, separate from long-horizon planning.
Keeps the scene, instruction, start pose, and route fixed while varying robot width to test passability-aware behavior.
Encodes body width via obstacle inflation in a depth-based local bird’s-eye view, fusing geometry, vision, and language to predict closed-loop actions.
Improves collision-free success by approximately 12 percentage points over a fine-tuned strong VLN baseline and generalizes to unseen widths.
Integration with a high-level planner yields higher success with fewer local commands; real-world deployment demonstrates low-level execution effectiveness.
papers.selection_reason: Passability-aware local-command benchmark and model for vision-and-language navigation.
papers.title: PASS-VLN: Passability-Aware Local-Command Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: PASS-VLN benchmarks and enables vision-language navigation that adapts local motion to robot body width, choosing to pass through feasible gaps or stop safely before blockages.

papers.abstract: Speed-limit sign recognition on an automotive camera system-on-chip (SoC) must fit a detector and a classifier (the reader) into the memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets of the device. In our two-stage recognizer, the detector, a YOLO-family network with ReLU and hard-sigmoid operators, is compressed by channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade identifies the channels to remove, the recorded deletions are replayed on the original task-trained network, the parent, and one continuous knowledge-distillation recovery follows. On a YOLOv5n, replay removes 60.3% of the parameters at the accuracy of the parent and, in validation mAP50-95 over five matched seeds, outperforms iterative pruning and training from scratch, and its per-step variant (per-step replay) is the most accurate pruning method. On a YOLOv8n, replay and per-step replay outperform every other method and the unpruned parent. The reader, a five-layer CNN with 18k parameters, and the post-processing of the YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n heads use integer arithmetic only. With 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W4A8), the reader matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory, and an executable streaming model reproduces the INT8 class predictions of its runtime on all 9,850 test crops. On a Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only in the implicit formulation of TensorRT, and the replay detector runs fastest on the deep-learning accelerator (DLA). Trained on public data only, the combined system of 0.72 M parameters recognizes 95.2% of the signs of a held-out automotive camera at 90% precision and 94 frames per second.
authors: Se Un Park, Kyungkeon Chung, Huigeol Kim, Junyoung Park
bullets: Channel replay removes 60.3% of YOLOv5n parameters while maintaining parent accuracy; replay variants outperform competing pruning methods on YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n.
A five-layer, 18k-parameter reader achieves FP32-equivalent accuracy with 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory.
Integer-only post-processing and reader inference support executable streaming deployment, reproducing runtime INT8 predictions on all 9,850 test crops.
The combined 0.72M-parameter system reaches 95.2% sign recognition at 90% precision and 94 frames per second on a held-out automotive camera.
On Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only for TensorRT’s implicit formulation; replay detection runs fastest on the DLA.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes replay pruning and few-bit integer inference for hardware-efficient speed-sign recognition, relevant to Efficient AI.
papers.title: Replay Pruning and Few-Bit Integer Inference for Hardware-Efficient Speed-Sign Recognition
papers.tldr: A replay-pruned detector and few-bit integer reader enable accurate, real-time speed-sign recognition within automotive SoC memory and compute constraints.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.
authors: Yining Li, Huayang Li, Lemao Liu, Taro Watanabe
bullets: Studies position bias in multiple-choice and multi-document tasks across five languages.
Covers models ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameter scales.
Finds position bias remains noticeable in small models and non-English languages.
Reports that larger models and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate the issue.
Extended-reasoning “thinking models” are nearly immune, though this may be costly.
papers.selection_reason: Comprehensive study of position bias in LLMs across scales and languages; relevant to LLM behavior and evaluation.
papers.title: On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
papers.tldr: Position bias is strongest in smaller models and non-English settings, but is reduced by scaling and Chain-of-Thought prompting, with thinking models showing near immunity.

papers.abstract: Reusing a Transformer block across depth increases computation without replicating its parameters, but successive passes have no dedicated state through which positions can exchange compact summaries of their causal prefix. We introduce the causal latent workspace Transformer: an anchored, four-round shared-depth architecture in which each position writes gated vectors into prefix-specific latent slots and retrieves a content-addressed summary before the next shared block application. This path complements causal self-attention while the original input embedding remains accessible at every round. Across three byte-level corpora, three seeds, and two matched parameter budgets, the proposed model achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings against five Transformer controls. At 101.71M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories, reaching perplexities 2.7820, 2.7843, and 1.6823; these improve upon the strongest non-workspace control on each corpus by 1.06%, 0.73%, and 1.01%. All nine seed-labelled comparisons at this budget favor the workspace. At 0.918M parameters it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories, whereas a conditioned loop is stronger on enwik8. Architectural ablations show that adding the workspace improves upon the anchored loop in all six settings and support refreshing its causal summaries at each round. Together, these results identify a causal, content-addressable prefix workspace as an effective structural augmentation of looped Transformers.
authors: Ilia Zaznov
bullets: Addresses the lack of dedicated state for causal prefix information in parameter-shared Transformer loops.
Uses an anchored four-round architecture with gated writes to causal latent slots and content-addressed retrieval before each shared block pass.
The workspace achieves the best mean held-out perplexity in five of six settings across three byte-level corpora and two parameter budgets.
At 101.71M parameters, it leads on WikiText-103 raw, enwik8, and TinyStories; at 0.918M, it leads on WikiText-103 and TinyStories.
Ablations show consistent gains over the anchored loop and support refreshing causal summaries each round; a conditioned loop remains stronger on small-budget enwik8.
papers.selection_reason: Looped Transformer architecture with causal latent workspace memory; fits LLM architecture and memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Causal Latent Workspaces for Looped Transformers
papers.tldr: A causal latent workspace improves shared-depth looped Transformers by letting positions exchange compact, prefix-specific summaries across repeated block applications.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
authors: Lieqi Liu, Rui gao, Jia-Chen Gu, Wenbo Hu, Zhaobin Mo, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar, Wei Wang, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Targets long-tail, safety-critical scenarios that existing perception and simple temporal benchmarks underrepresent.
Covers six task families, including spatial reasoning, temporal memory and extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness.
Combines multiple-choice judgments with free-form VQA requiring scene explanations and driving-decision justifications.
Across 12 models, the best reported average multiple-choice accuracy is 43.4%, compared with an approximately 20% random-choice baseline.
Finds that descriptive scene understanding does not guarantee accurate safety judgments, with motion reconstruction especially challenging.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces STRIDE, a benchmark for spatiotemporal reasoning in driving edge cases, highly relevant to VLMs and Video Understanding.
papers.title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases
papers.tldr: STRIDE benchmarks whether vision-language models can reason about object motion, interactions, and future consequences in complex driving edge cases.

papers.abstract: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3\% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132.
authors: Xinyu Luo, Jincheng Zhou, Mengbo Wang, Zilin Shen, Nadia Atallah Lanman, Petros Drineas, Bruno Ribeiro, Brian Bullins
bullets: Targets the stale-subspace problem in gradient-projecting low-rank optimizers such as GaLore.
Uses an Oja++-inspired streaming $k$-PCA algorithm for frequent, on-the-fly tracking of principal gradient directions.
Reduces the performance gap to full-rank optimization by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task.
Achieves the best performance in 10 of 16 RoBERTa-Base fine-tuning scenarios.
Designed for stringent low-rank constraints with low per-step tracking cost.
papers.selection_reason: Streaming low-rank gradient subspace tracking reduces LLM training memory.
papers.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
papers.tldr: Ori tracks slowly drifting gradient subspaces online with streaming $k$-PCA, improving very low-rank LLM training toward full-rank accuracy.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on proprietary records enables domain adaptation but introduces two challenges: (i) privacy leakage of memorized private data, such as personally identifiable information (PII), and (ii) balancing private data removal with utility preservation. Existing defenses, including data sanitization and differential privacy, often degrade performance, while privacy-neuron editing lacks a PII-free reference to distinguish identity-specific neurons from those supporting useful text. We propose JEPA-Prune, a post-hoc neuron pruning framework guided by a model trained exclusively on PII-free views. Alongside the fine-tuned private model, JEPA-Prune, trains a public model on surrogate and masked views of the same records using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), capturing domain knowledge without identifiers. A cross-model representation probe quantifies deviations between private representations of leaked records and this PII-free reference. Integrated gradients and a scale-invariant specificity score then identify PII-responsive neurons, which are pruned without retraining. Experiments show that pruning just 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4x and PII extraction recall by up to 13.9x, while keeping unseen-text perplexity within 16% of that of the unpruned model for most LLMs. In contrast, privacy-neuron editing increases perplexity by at least 26x.
authors: Mohamed Shaaban, Mohamed Elmahallawy
bullets: Fine-tuning on proprietary records can memorize PII, creating a privacy–utility trade-off.
JEPA-Prune trains a PII-free public reference model on surrogate and masked views of the same records.
Cross-model representation probing, integrated gradients, and a scale-invariant specificity score identify neurons associated with PII.
Pruning 1.6% of neurons reduces PII inference accuracy by up to 7.4× and extraction recall by up to 13.9×.
Unseen-text perplexity generally remains within 16% of the unpruned model, outperforming privacy-neuron editing in utility preservation.
papers.selection_reason: Post-hoc neuron pruning for privacy in fine-tuned LLMs; relevant to LLM methods and model editing.
papers.title: Prune the Leaky Neurons: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in Fine-Tuned LLMs via Joint-Embedding-Guided Pruning
papers.tldr: JEPA-Prune reduces private-data leakage in fine-tuned LLMs by pruning a small set of PII-responsive neurons while largely preserving language-model utility.

papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive decoding advances one token at a time, even when several upcoming tokens can be predicted together. We propose CADENCE (Context-Adaptive DEcoding), a generation method that learns both what to draft and how far to draft. Gaussian prediction heads represent future spans as continuous latent vectors, and a shared decoder converts the selected vector into token predictions in parallel. A learned router selects the prediction length from the model's own hidden states and predicted Gaussian parameters, adapting generation granularity to the current context with single-token generation as a fallback. The backbone verifies each proposed continuation and retains the prefix that matches its greedy predictions. Experiments with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval show that router-selected positions yield higher draft acceptance than applying the corresponding prediction length everywhere. CADENCE achieves up to 1.3x higher generation throughput than standard greedy decoding.
authors: Sai Sreenivas Chintha, Chidera Biringa, Rishab Sharma, Anusha Agrawal, Prachi Badarayani, Gemma Zhang, Nigel Boachie Kumankumah, Marco Ayala, Sulaiman Vesal
bullets: Standard decoding generates one token at a time despite predictable multi-token continuations.
Gaussian prediction heads encode future spans as continuous latent vectors, which a shared decoder converts into parallel token predictions.
A learned router selects the draft length from hidden states and Gaussian parameters, with single-token decoding as a fallback.
The backbone verifies drafts and keeps the prefix matching its greedy predictions.
On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across Alpaca, GSM8K, and HumanEval, CADENCE achieves up to 1.3× higher throughput than greedy decoding; adaptive routing also improves draft acceptance over fixed lengths.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive decoding length improves LLM generation throughput.
papers.title: Next Token or Vector? Learning How Far to Decode
papers.tldr: CADENCE accelerates autoregressive generation by adaptively choosing how many future tokens to draft and verify at each step.

papers.abstract: N-dimensional splatting extends 3D Gaussian Splatting with view direction and time to model view-dependent and dynamic effects. Each primitive is lifted into a joint distribution over position and conditioning variables, then conditionally sliced at each rendering query. N-DGS and UBS share this step across Gaussian and Beta kernels: recovering the conditional mean, opacity, and covariance requires per-primitive matrix inversions and regression products in every forward pass. We introduce direct conditional parameterization, replacing this covariance-derived readout with explicit per-effect parameters: a Cholesky precision factor for opacity and a factorized query-to-position regression operator with learnable per-dimension coupling. Unrestricted conditional coordinates recover a valid joint covariance; our factorization adds spatial-scale and coupling priors. Applied to both kernels, the parameterization yields dGS (Gaussian) and dBS (Beta). Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, they match or exceed their covariance-derived counterparts on quality, with gains up to +1.26 dB in the main MCMC evaluation. Production slicing is 6.9-7.7 times faster than on-the-fly covariance-derived conditioning; complete-render profiling gives 1.25-1.91 times speedups on four trained scenes. Direct conditioning provides a structured, kernel-agnostic alternative for N-dimensional splatting. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/dgs/.
authors: Zhongpai Gao, Benjamin Planche, Van Nguyen Nguyen, Meng Zheng, Anwesa Choudhuri, Arun Innanje, Terrence Chen, Ziyan Wu
bullets: N-dimensional splatting models view-dependent and dynamic effects by conditioning primitives on query variables.
The method replaces per-query covariance inversions and regression products with explicit Cholesky precision and factorized query-to-position parameters.
Applied to Gaussian and Beta kernels, it produces dGS and dBS with structured spatial-scale and coupling priors.
Across five static and dynamic benchmarks, quality matches or exceeds covariance-derived methods, with gains up to 1.26 dB.
Production slicing is 6.9–7.7× faster, while complete rendering is 1.25–1.91× faster on four trained scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces direct conditional parameterization for N-dimensional splatting, a significant technical contribution to 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: Direct Conditional Parameterization for N-Dimensional Splatting
papers.tldr: Direct conditional parameterization makes N-dimensional Gaussian and Beta splatting substantially faster while matching or improving rendering quality.

papers.abstract: Scale calibration learns an update for one model representation. We study how much of that update can be reused by another representation of the same pretrained model. Our transfer procedure extracts positive group-wise gains and installs them in the recipient's weights or native quantization scales without recipient-side optimization. On a quantized recipient, it preserves integer codes, zero points and storage layout. For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, bidirectional transfer retains 76.9-90.5% of the text-loss improvement from recipient-specific calibration on fresh WikiText and C4 cohorts excluded from project development. Shuffling the same gain values within each projection worsens both recipients, showing that their learned group assignment matters after transfer. A Llama-3.2-3B control keeps the initial native tensors at all four calibrated projections identical and changes nine projections elsewhere. Cross-installation retains 98.6-99.3% of the text-calibration benefit, alongside a small, resolved preference for each recipient's own gain. These results quantify both the adaptation carried by a reusable calibration update and the remaining benefit of recipient-specific training.
authors: Xu Cao, Wenxuan Xiao
bullets: Problem: Determine whether calibration updates learned for one model representation can be reused by another representation.
Method: Extract positive group-wise gains and install them into recipient weights or native quantization scales while preserving quantized codes, zero points, and storage layout.
Main result: For a Qwen3-1.7B floating-point/GPTQ INT3 pair, transfer retained 76.9–90.5% of recipient-specific text-loss improvement on held-out WikiText and C4 cohorts.
Shuffling gain values within projections degraded both recipients, indicating that learned group assignments are important.
A Llama-3.2-3B control retained 98.6–99.3% of text-calibration benefit after cross-installation, with a small remaining preference for recipient-specific gains.
papers.selection_reason: Quantization calibration transfer improves memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Reusing Calibration Gains across Model Representations
papers.tldr: Calibration gains learned for one representation can be transferred to another representation of the same pretrained model, preserving most of recipient-specific calibration benefits without recipient-side optimization.

papers.abstract: Precise pedicel-targeted grasping in strawberry harvesting remains a critical bottleneck due to the pedicel's small diameter (1.3-3 mm), color similarity with surrounding foliage, and precise force control required for clean abscission zone detachment. As a market-grade crop, strawberry aesthetic value makes bruise-free pedicel detachment essential over direct fruit grasping. Classical approaches struggle to unify vision models, motion planning, and contact manipulation into a robust framework, particularly in occluded canopy environments. Therefore, this work presents a visuomotor imitation learning pipeline for pedicel-targeted strawberry harvesting that unifies perception, motion planning, and contact manipulation from collecting human teleoperation demonstrations, training an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy with a ResNet-50 visual backbone, and deploying the learned policy autonomously on a Jetson AGX Orin edge platform at 15 Hz. The trained policy achieved consistent loss convergence from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100K gradient steps on 130 demonstrations. We have also established a reproducible open-source pipeline with publicly released dataset and model weights for the agricultural robotics community. Full dataset is available at, https://huggingface.co/datasets/nitindominicrai/strawberry_pedicel_grasp_teleoperation and trained policy at, https://huggingface.co/nitindominicrai/act_strawberry_pedicel. To replicate this work, all code, configurations, and deployment instructions are publicly available at, https://github.com/nitin-dominic/autonomous_strawberry_pedicel_harvesting.
authors: Nitin Rai, Won Suk Lee, Hongyoung Leon, Heping Zhu
bullets: Addresses precise, bruise-free pedicel detachment in visually challenging strawberry canopies.
Learns from human teleoperation demonstrations using an ACT policy with a ResNet-50 visual backbone.
Runs autonomously at 15 Hz on a Jetson AGX Orin edge platform.
Training loss decreased from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100K steps using 130 demonstrations.
Reproducible code, dataset, model weights, and deployment instructions are publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Imitation learning pipeline for robotic manipulation and grasping in strawberry harvesting.
papers.title: Pedicel-Targeted Strawberry Harvesting via Imitation Learning on a Low-Cost Teleoperated Robotic Arm
papers.tldr: An imitation-learning pipeline enables a low-cost robotic arm to target strawberry pedicels by combining visual perception, motion planning, and contact manipulation.

papers.abstract: Rigid-body motion planning is fundamental to robotic transport and manipulation, where both object position and orientation determine whether a body can move through cluttered environments. This coupling makes planning chal- lenging because translation and rotation can be constrained very differently by surrounding geometry. We propose Shape- Aware Neural Time Fields, a physics-informed neural motion planning framework that learns a reusable travel-time, or cost- to-go, representation for rigid-body motion while explicitly accounting for these distinct geometric restrictions. The learned field captures local motion difficulty in translation and rotation and is paired with a sampling-based planner that balances progress toward the goal with the cost of reaching nearby poses. We evaluate the framework across 2D and 3D rigid- body planning tasks and non-prehensile manipulation through object pushing in diverse environments. Results show substantial improvements in planning success and inference efficiency over physics-informed neural planning baselines, while remaining competitive with classical sampling-based planners at significantly lower planning times. Ablation studies further validate the contributions of both the learned representation and the proposed planning strategy. Finally, closed-loop pushing experiments under execution deviations and external disturbances demonstrate that fast replanning enables reactive and adaptive task execution.
authors: Yanming Zhou, Yuchen Liu, Ahmed H. Qureshi
bullets: Targets rigid-body planning where position and orientation face different geometric constraints in cluttered environments.
Learns a reusable physics-informed travel-time/cost-to-go field capturing local difficulty in translation and rotation.
Combines the learned field with a sampling-based planner that balances goal progress against nearby-pose reachability costs.

Evaluated on 2D/3D planning and non-prehensile pushing, with improved success and inference efficiency over physics-informed neural baselines and competitiveness with classical planners at lower planning times.
Closed-loop pushing experiments show that fast replanning supports adaptation to execution deviations and external disturbances.
papers.selection_reason: Learned shape-aware neural time fields for rigid-body motion and non-prehensile manipulation planning; directly fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Shape-Aware Neural Time Fields for Rigid-Body Motion and Manipulation Planning
papers.tldr: A shape-aware neural time field enables faster, reactive rigid-body motion and pushing plans by modeling translation and rotation constraints separately.

papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are trained predominantly on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images but are increasingly used as frozen feature extractors for immunohistochemistry (IHC), where cross-hospital differences can impair grading. However, systematic comparisons of correction methods for cross-hospital IHC grading remain limited. To address this gap, we benchmark label-free transformations applied to input images before frozen-FM encoding and to features after frozen-FM encoding using UNI and Virchow2, three IHC markers, and six directed cross-hospital transfers, yielding 12 settings. Among the evaluated input-space methods, our proposed method FIX achieved the largest macro-F1 improvement over no correction, outperforming well-known stain normalization techniques. Among feature-space methods, a simple feature-wise standardization achieved the best improvement over no correction, outperforming CORAL. Under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation, combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) by 0.181 and 0.208, respectively, and reduced ordinal error by 0.209 relative to no correction. These results show that input- and feature-space transformations can provide complementary benefits for cross-hospital IHC grading with frozen pathology FMs.
authors: Jongwoon Lee, Jhair Gallardo, Christopher Kanan
bullets: Cross-hospital variation can impair IHC grading when H&E-trained foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors.
The study benchmarks input-space corrections and feature-space corrections with UNI and Virchow2 across three IHC markers and six directed hospital transfers.
FIX achieved the strongest improvement among input-space methods, while feature-wise standardization outperformed CORAL in feature space.
Combining FIX with feature-wise standardization improved macro-F1 and QWK and reduced ordinal error under patient-averaged tile-level evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes input and feature space corrections for cross-hospital pathology foundation models, relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models and domain adaptation.
papers.title: Input- and Feature-Space Correction for Cross-Hospital IHC Grading
papers.tldr: Label-free corrections applied before and after frozen pathology foundation models improve cross-hospital IHC grading, with complementary gains from combining both.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) for visual question answering (VQA) often pass long visual-token sequences to the language model, making visual-token pruning attractive but risky for medical images, where answers may depend on localized boundary and texture evidence. We study training free pre-decoding pruning and treat pruning as a subspace stable evidence preservation problem. The retained tokens should remain close to the dominant visual evidence subspace induced by the full token set. To this end, we propose \emph{Subspace-Transition Token Pruning} (\method{}), which estimates each token's spectral support from principal component space and constructs a compact representation subspace. To better reflect medical image structure, \method{} further uses a bounded token-grid transition prior to promote boundary and texture sensitive tokens. We evaluate \method{} on the closed-ended SLAKE and OmniMedVQA benchmarks and on RadImageNet-VQA, which provides both closed-ended and open-ended evaluations, using Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones. \method{} delivers consistently strong performance on both the closed-ended and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations. These results show that \method{} is an effective training free pruning framework for medical domain VQA.
authors: Mengchen Fan, Qizhen Lan, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Liang He, Tianyang Wang, Xiaoqian Jiang, Pulin Che, Baocheng Geng
bullets: Medical VQA often uses long visual-token sequences, but pruning can remove localized evidence needed for accurate answers.
MedSTP estimates tokens’ support in principal-component space to preserve the dominant visual evidence subspace.
A bounded token-grid transition prior promotes tokens capturing medical-image boundaries and textures.
Evaluated on SLAKE, OmniMedVQA, and RadImageNet-VQA with Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B.
It shows consistently strong performance on both closed- and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses token pruning in medical VLMs using subspace stability, directly relevant to Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: MedSTP: Preserving Subspace and Transition Evidence for Medical VQA Token Pruning
papers.tldr: MedSTP is a training-free medical VQA token-pruning method that preserves dominant visual evidence while retaining boundary- and texture-sensitive tokens.

papers.abstract: Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce $R^2$-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.
authors: Xiaoyan Cong, Tianyu Wang, Hyeonho Jeong, Zhifei Zhang, Yuqian Zhou, Yijun Li, Shaoteng Liu, Zhe Lin, Srinath Sridhar, Soo Ye Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of controlling video edits with variable combinations and numbers of multimodal references.
Uses a reference-bank interface, R²-RoPE for reference scalability, and a single-stream diffusion transformer with MLLM-derived context.
Builds synthetic OmniXRef-Data and applies curriculum learning to handle limited video-reference editing data and increasing task complexity.
Introduces OmniXRef-Bench for evaluating video-reference attribute transfer across camera, motion, content, style, and VFX.
Reports better performance than task-specific baselines and commercial models in comprehensive evaluations.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal multi-reference video editing with a diffusion transformer, directly relevant to video diffusion and editing.
papers.title: OmniXRef: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Multi-Reference Video Editing
papers.tldr: OmniXRef unifies text, image, and video references for flexible, multi-attribute video editing in one framework.

papers.abstract: Spatial memory enables robots to reuse past observations for localization, navigation, and question answering. Designing such memory involves jointly deciding what to retain and how to retrieve it for diverse semantic, metric, and temporal needs. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent. The resulting implementations are frozen before building memories from held-out observation histories, without access to downstream questions, and evaluated across five complementary task tracks using the same Query Agent. Across three independent design searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra averages 44.23 on the equally weighted five-track score, versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, the strongest evaluated baseline supporting all five tracks, a 50.9% relative improvement. Qualitative analysis relates performance differences to evidence retention and retrieval, while identifying grounding and evidence-use failures. These results demonstrate the potential of coding agents to automate spatial memory design, while revealing task-dependent trade-offs in performance and computational cost. Project page: https://ba-fa-3344.github.io/.
authors: Qianwei Wang, Ce Zhang, Zhanpeng Luo, Pengpeng Su, Shuo Yang, Hao Xu
bullets: Spatial memory must retain and retrieve observations for semantic, metric, and temporal tasks.
A Designer Agent iteratively implements and evaluates memory construction and retrieval with feedback from a fixed Query Agent.
Designs are frozen before evaluation on held-out observation histories and five task tracks, without access to downstream questions.
Across three searches, Codex / GPT-6 Astra scores 44.23 versus 29.32 for ReMEmbR, a 50.9% relative improvement.
Analysis identifies evidence-retention and retrieval differences, plus grounding and evidence-use failures; performance remains task-dependent.
papers.selection_reason: Automated design of spatial memory for robots directly fits embodied memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Spatial Memory by Agents, for Agents
papers.tldr: Coding agents can automatically design spatial memories for robots, substantially improving multi-task performance while exposing trade-offs in grounding, evidence use, and computational cost.

papers.abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.
authors: Aaron J. Li, Weijia Xu, Chandan Singh, Zixiao Chen, Jeevana Priya Inala, Charlotte Siska, Acar Tamersoy, Bin Yu, Ion Stoica, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
bullets: Evaluates agents on continuous, multi-task development and maintenance workflows rather than isolated tasks.
Uses an external black-box controller to inject useful operational micro-skills, prune persistently irrelevant tools, and interrupt unproductive failure loops.
Reduces average token costs by 18.4–30.9% across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI with frontier models, with savings reported for every tested repository and agent-model setting.
Generalizes to sequential web development and security auditing, yielding cost reductions of 6.4–21.2% depending on task structure.
The approach targets environment-dependent recurring costs and is evaluated within the tested agents, repositories, and domains.
papers.selection_reason: Black-box token cost control for coding agents, reducing compute cost under Efficient AI.
papers.title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
papers.tldr: TokenEconomizer adaptively reduces coding-agent token costs across sequences of realistic software-engineering tasks while maintaining comparable success.

papers.abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attacker, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here, it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
authors: Georgios Politis, Evangelos Pappas
bullets: Addresses inconsistent evaluations caused by differing attacker access, model knowledge, datasets, and recovery metrics.
Records messages and attack settings so compatible attacks can be reused, independently scored, and compared.
Requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass and separates implementation checks from attack effectiveness.
In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding training-time gradients increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%.
Supports further analysis of corpus choice, compression defences, attack implementations, and measurement code; claims should state controls and untested attacks.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LLM-Attacker, a framework for evaluating privacy in split and distributed LLM systems. It provides a unified approach to red-teaming LLM architectures.
papers.title: The LLM-Attacker: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
papers.tldr: LLM-Attacker standardizes and audits privacy evaluations for split and distributed LLMs by tracking attacker assumptions, enabling reproducible comparisons, and exposing untested attacks.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning aims to forget certain information while preserving others, without retraining from scratch. SoTA methods such as NPO, SimNPO, and SatImp balance forgetting and retain through whole model fine-tuning, while FOM-UL explores selective layer updates. Prior works show that suppressing target information can damage retained knowledge. This trade-off can vary across layers even under the same unlearning loss. In this work, we propose Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning (CoLU), which combines a novel confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating a single selected transformer layer, rather than the whole model for unlearning. To reduce CoLU compute cost, we further propose Brief Layer Screening (BLS), which uses a newly defined normalized forgetting-retention (NFR) score to first rank layers through a brief unlearning trials using a subset of forgetting dataset and fewer epochs. BLS pre-selects top-k ranked layer candidates, which will then be fully profiled using full data analysis. BLS is proven to reduce the runtime of CoLU by 60.2-79.7% with almost the same performance. On TOFU dataset, CoLU improves both forgetting and retention over NPO, SatImp, and GA-based FOM-UL in all six TOFU settings, and over SimNPO in five of the six settings. On MUSE Books and News datasets, CoLU achieves the highest retained KnowMem and the PrivLeak closest to zero among the compared SOTA unlearning methods. CoLU presents a new record performance in both unlearning and retain in most settings up to date. Moreover, across the measured settings, average CoLU GPU memory usage is 77.4% to 79.5% lower than full-model unlearning.
authors: Jingkai Guo, Ziyi Zhao, Chaitali Chakrabarti, Deliang Fan
bullets: Addresses the risk that suppressing target information damages retained knowledge, with trade-offs varying across layers.
Uses confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating only a selected layer.
Brief Layer Screening (BLS) ranks candidate layers using a normalized forgetting-retention score before full profiling.
BLS reduces CoLU runtime by 60.2–79.7% with nearly unchanged performance.
Across TOFU, MUSE Books, and News, CoLU generally improves forgetting and retention while using 77.4–79.5% less GPU memory than full-model unlearning.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes CoLU, a layerwise unlearning method for LLMs. It balances forgetting and retention by updating specific layers, contributing to the understanding of LLM memory and adaptation.
papers.title: CoLU: Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning for Large Language Models
papers.tldr: CoLU improves LLM unlearning–retention trade-offs by updating one confidence-selected transformer layer, while BLS sharply reduces layer-screening cost.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity 3D generative modeling underpins game asset creation, medical imaging, and VR/AR environmental design, where geometric structure directly influences perception and decision-making. Diffusion models represent a powerful paradigm for point cloud generation. However, existing approaches rely heavily on local voxel or patch features and often miss global structural organization, and much less work has studied how global conditioning can be used to improve generation quality. In this paper, we introduce HilbertGen-3D, a novel topology-aware conditional diffusion framework based on Hilbert-Multifractal Conditioning (HMC). HMC computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them via a 3D Hilbert curve to expose structured spatial dependencies, and estimates the generalized fractal dimensions from scale-dependent partition functions. We encode these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, and inject them into a diffusion denoiser through an efficient bottleneck fusion module. Across the Chair, Airplane, and Car categories of ShapeNet, our two conditioning variants reduce the absolute deviation of 1-Nearest Neighbor Accuracy (1-NNA) from 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and increase coverage by up to 5.88 percentage points relative to TopoDiT-3D. This shows that combining local density cues with global Hilbert-multifractal structure provides a simple and effective recipe for high-fidelity and diverse 3D generation.
authors: Ziyi Zhang, Shixuan Li, Yorie Nakahira, Paul Bogdan, Guannan Qu
bullets: Addresses the inability of local voxel or patch features to capture global geometric organization in 3D generation.
Computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them with a 3D Hilbert curve, and estimates generalized fractal dimensions.
Encodes these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, fused into the diffusion denoiser through a bottleneck module.
On ShapeNet Chair, Airplane, and Car categories, it improves 1-NNA closeness to 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and coverage by up to 5.88 points versus TopoDiT-3D.
Scope is limited to the reported ShapeNet categories and two proposed conditioning variants.
papers.selection_reason: Topology-aware conditional diffusion for 3D point cloud generation, fitting 3D generative modeling.
papers.title: HilbertGen-3D:Hilbert--Multifractal Conditioning for Topology-Aware 3D Generation
papers.tldr: HilbertGen-3D improves topology-aware 3D point-cloud generation by conditioning diffusion models on global multi-scale Hilbert–multifractal structure alongside local density cues.

papers.abstract: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at $8\times$ the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about $25\%$.
authors: Yuxuan Liu
bullets: Addresses the limitation of monotonic decay mechanisms that cannot erase intermediate tokens selectively.
Uses path extrema: logits are penalized according to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field across the key–query span.
Includes the Forgetting Transformer as a special case; under a shared learned walk, unpenalized keys form a stack.
A constant-dimensional FPA head can realize arbitrary subsets of surviving keys, unlike comparable softmax-based mechanisms requiring dimension linear in key count.
In experiments, FPA converges to target key sets, matches FoX perplexity, and achieves perfect passkey retrieval at 8× training length with a cache compressed to about 25%.
papers.selection_reason: Novel attention mechanism with forget gates and KV cache compression, directly relevant to efficient attention and memory.
papers.title: First Passage Attention
papers.tldr: First Passage Attention enables selective forgetting of intermediate context while preserving older relevant tokens, outperforming comparable mechanisms on synthetic memory tasks and long-context passkey retrieval.

papers.abstract: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.
authors: Nicholas Saban, Charvi Bannur, Mariya Vasileva, Darshan Deshpande
bullets: Covers five domains and 19 simulation skills, evaluating state-transition prediction from full agent trajectories.
Compares model predictions with execution-derived references using deterministic checks and a semantic judge.
Across 20 general-purpose and specialized models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest reported success rate at 49.57%.
Performance drops sharply when actions affect dependent objects, with average success of 5.1% on such tasks.
631 tasks remain unsolved by every evaluated model, highlighting substantial world-modeling gaps.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for text-based world models predicting action-conditioned environment transitions; fits interactive world models.
papers.title: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations
papers.tldr: GlobeBench introduces a 1,632-task benchmark showing that current language models struggle to predict complex, cascading changes in text-based environments.

papers.abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.
authors: Faizan Siddiqui, Nirav Savaliya, Sahith Reddy Chada, Enna Sachdeva
bullets: Addresses the lack of stable spatial context in video MLLMs that primarily organize observations over time.
Back-projects visual patch features using depth and camera pose into shared BEV coordinates, averaging features within spatial cells.
Compresses 128 frames and roughly 100K patch features into 729 BEV tokens without architectural changes beyond tokenization.
Reduces LLM prefill time by 2.9× and peak memory by 3.6×.
Outperforms the matched frame-token control on VSI-Bench and ReVSI, with especially strong VSI-Bench gains in room-size and relative-direction reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: BEV tokenization compresses video MLLM visual tokens while improving embodied spatial reasoning, combining spatial intelligence, token merging, and video understanding.
papers.title: Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens
papers.tldr: Cambrian-BEV improves embodied spatial reasoning by aggregating multi-view video features into a compact, persistent bird’s-eye-view representation.

papers.abstract: We study personalized LLM routing, where a router selects among heterogeneous models with different costs and capabilities. The router must minimize cumulative inference cost while ensuring reliable realized response quality, even though user preferences are unknown and must be learned from feedback during deployment. We formulate this problem as a constrained contextual bandit and develop an algorithm that learns preferences while balancing cost and quality. Under a logistic preference model and a strict-feasibility condition, we establish sublinear expected cost regret relative to an optimal stationary randomized contextual oracle and a high-probability guarantee on realized cumulative satisfaction. The framework extends beyond LLM routing to broader online model-selection problems with reliability requirements.
authors: Ameya Anjarlekar, Rasoul Etesami, R Srikant
bullets: Addresses personalized routing across heterogeneous LLMs with different costs and capabilities.
Models routing as a constrained contextual bandit with unknown preferences learned from deployment feedback.
Uses chance constraints to control realized cumulative user satisfaction, not just expected quality.
Under a logistic preference model and strict feasibility, proves sublinear expected cost regret and high-probability satisfaction guarantees.
Applies more broadly to online model selection with reliability requirements.
papers.selection_reason: Cost-aware LLM routing with reliability constraints reduces inference cost.
papers.title: Chance-Constrained Personalized LLM Routing with Online Preference Learning
papers.tldr: An online contextual-bandit router learns user preferences to minimize LLM inference costs while maintaining reliable response quality.

papers.abstract: Agents operating over long horizons need an effective memory that allows them to reuse their experience throughout long interactions. If the entire history of an interaction is retained, it becomes difficult to find the relevant experience, while compressing it into summaries may result in the loss of visual and spatial details that are required later on. We present \textbf{MFM}, a multimodal filesystem memory architecture that keeps complementary types of agent memory. \textbf{Episodic memory} stores the observations, actions, and outcomes, and \textbf{spatial memory} associates experiences with locations. \textbf{Semantic and procedural memory} build up general knowledge and reusable methods of acting, and \textbf{working memory} holds the current plans. MFM makes use of searchable textual records to connect these different representations to the underlying multimodal episodes. The agents are able to find previous experiences by means of contextual cues and to examine the original observations in order to recover details that are missing from their textual descriptions. Through consolidation, the agents convert experience into higher-level knowledge and procedures while still keeping references to the original episodes. In the case of long-horizon Minecraft and computer-use tasks, MFM leads to improved performance with three base models. With GPT-6-Astra, MFM completes \emph{Mine Diamond from Scratch} and reaches 16 out of 24 milestones on the \emph{Ender Dragon} task, as against 12.7 for the best baseline. On CUABench-KiCad it attains a mean reward of 0.440, as compared to 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 in the case of no persistent memory.
authors: Chloe Su, Jiahan Li, Zhenting Qi, Chaoran Cheng, Haoyu Chen, Sejoon Jun, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of retrieving relevant history while preserving visual and spatial details over long interactions.
Combines episodic, spatial, semantic, procedural, and working memory in a filesystem-based architecture.
Uses searchable textual records to retrieve experiences and inspect their underlying multimodal observations.
Consolidates experiences into reusable knowledge and procedures while retaining links to source episodes.
Improves results across three base models, including stronger performance on long-horizon Minecraft and CUABench-KiCad tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal filesystem memory for long-horizon embodied agents, directly matching embodied memory.
papers.title: Multimodal Filesystem Memory For Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: MFM gives long-horizon embodied agents a searchable multimodal memory that links textual knowledge to original visual-spatial experiences, improving performance on Minecraft and computer-use tasks.

papers.abstract: Answering complex spatial reasoning questions from egocentric video requires determining what evidence is needed, acquiring targeted observations, and combining them through multiple reasoning steps. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to perform this process reliably. Agentic systems address this challenge by querying external vision and geometry tools, but training their reasoning leaves these tools unchanged, so inaccurate observations can still lead to incorrect answers. We introduce EgoP$^{2}$C, a framework that internalizes a plan-perceive-compose process within a single VLM. To this end, we first train specialized Planner and Perception teachers using separate adapters (Dual-LoRA), then fine-tune the corresponding experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) student under their supervision. We subsequently train the student on trajectories generated by its current policy using a segment-level extension of multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), assigning different trajectory segments to different supervisors. The Planner teacher supervises which evidence-seeking questions to ask, when to stop gathering evidence, and how to compose the final answer. The Perception teacher supervises the video-grounded answers to those questions. At inference, the student executes this adaptive workflow end-to-end, without external spatial tools. Across three spatial reasoning benchmarks, EgoP$^{2}$C students built from Qwen3-VL-8B and SenseNova-SI-1.3-8B outperform their base models by an average of 9.2 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. Across both backbones, EgoP$^{2}$C reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8-66.3% and achieves $1.29$-$1.49\times$ speedups over their shared Dual-LoRA teacher.
authors: Chaoyu Li, Arka Sadhu, Yuliang Li, Hyo Jin Kim, Yuning Chai, Pooyan Fazli
bullets: Addresses unreliable multi-step spatial reasoning caused by inaccurate external tool observations.
Uses Planner and Perception teachers with Dual-LoRA to supervise a mixture-of-experts student.
Applies segment-level multi-teacher on-policy distillation to train the student on its own trajectories.
The resulting workflow adaptively asks evidence-seeking questions, stops gathering evidence, and composes final answers.
Across three benchmarks, it improves base-model accuracy by 9.2 and 7.5 points, reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8–66.3%, and achieves 1.29–1.49× speedups over the teachers.
papers.selection_reason: Internalizes plan-perceive-compose reasoning for egocentric video spatial understanding, fitting spatial intelligence and video-language reasoning.
papers.title: EgoP$^{2}$C: Internalizing Plan-Perceive-Compose for Spatial Reasoning in Egocentric Video
papers.tldr: EgoP²C teaches a single VLM to plan, selectively perceive, and compose answers for spatial reasoning in egocentric video without external tools.

papers.abstract: As assistants move from reactive answering toward proactive intervention, memory changes role: it no longer only supplies the answer to a query, it determines whether and when to speak at all. Prior work in this setting hands the system the relevant fact in context; we study the regime that makes the problem hard, where the evidence justifying an intervention must be mined from a long-horizon personal memory. We introduce ProPerMem, a benchmark for memory-driven proactive assistance (MPA), pairing egocentric video with year-long, distractor-rich user memories (~618K tokens on average), human-verified trigger windows, and a protocol that scores content and timing jointly. Every baseline we evaluate performs poorly (at most 15%), including frontier models given summarized or retrieval-augmented memory. A controlled study explains why: with oracle evidence delivered inside the trigger window GPT-5.3-Chat reaches 96%; letting it choose the timing drops it to 38%, and replacing oracle evidence with retrieval drops it to 15%. Content and timing are separately necessary, and missing either is catastrophic. Guided by this, we build ProPerAgent (Proactive Personalized Agent) with a plug-and-play harness that surfaces memory from a graph-organized store and gates it down to what is worth interrupting for, plus a lightweight RL stage that curbs early and repeated firing. Without any training, ProPerAgent lifts strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5% on Qwen3.8-27B and 38% on GPT-5.3-Chat; RL post-training reaches 42.4%.
authors: Shenglai Zeng, Xiao Yang, Tiffany Ma, Xinyuan Zhang, Nanshu Wang, Deren Lei, Kai Sun, Xilun Chen, Tammy Stark, Xianhui Zhu, Yuetai Li, Rulin Shao, Tianxin Wei, Rakesh Wanga, Anuj Kumar, Jiliang Tang, Wen-tau Yih, Xin Luna Dong
bullets: Introduces ProPerMem, a benchmark combining egocentric video, year-long distractor-rich memories, verified trigger windows, and joint content-timing evaluation.
Shows that both evidence retrieval and intervention timing are essential: performance collapses when either is not provided by an oracle.
Presents ProPerAgent, which uses graph-organized memory retrieval and interruption gating, followed by lightweight reinforcement learning to reduce premature and repeated interventions.
Improves strict accuracy from below 10% to 37.5–38% without training, and to 42.4% after RL post-training.
Scope: evaluated results remain substantially below oracle-evidence performance, highlighting the difficulty of long-horizon memory retrieval and timing.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-driven proactive assistance with long-horizon personal memory and egocentric video, fitting LLM/agent memory.
papers.title: ProPerAgent: Toward Memory-Driven Proactive Assistance
papers.tldr: ProPerAgent enables memory-driven proactive assistance by jointly retrieving the right personal evidence and deciding when an intervention is worth making.

papers.abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.
authors: Zihao Zhao, Avi Schwarzschild, Casey Meehan, Katherine Lee, Zhili Feng, Dylan Sam
bullets: Direct finetuning achieves the strongest capabilities but causes the most privacy leakage.
DP-SGD reduces leakage substantially, but with significant capability costs.
Synthetic-data generation, especially uniqueness-aware rewriting, provides a more favorable balance.
Privacy-aware rewriting outperforms naive paraphrasing for privacy protection across rewriting models.
More capable rewriting models generally lower downstream leakage, but held-out fit and extra test-time compute show inconsistent trends.
papers.selection_reason: Explores the empirical privacy landscape of training LLMs on synthetic data, comparing data-level and training-level interventions. This is relevant to LLM training methodologies and safety.
papers.title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data
papers.tldr: A controlled study finds that privacy-aware synthetic-data rewriting offers a better capability–privacy trade-off than direct finetuning or DP-SGD on synthetic medical records.

papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that switching optimizers between pretraining and subsequent training stages incurs a performance cost, but systematic investigation of this phenomenon is lacking. We study the mismatch between AdamW and Muon optimizers by pretraining 1.2B Llama-3 models from scratch while varying the proportion of updates taken with each optimizer, and similarly interpolating between the two optimizers during continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning (SFT).
