In Gemma 3 270M the embedding table holds 168M of 268M parameters, and because quantisation methods leave the embedding in 16-bit, it is also most of the file once the rest of the model is compressed. We ask what that table actually buys. We replace it with one frozen table of 512-bit codes, 16 MB, with no trainable parameters, derived once from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarisation, and we train the same Gemma-shaped body from scratch on the same 2.05B tokens with and without it. The learned table buys 0.20 nats of validation loss for 2.6 times the trainable parameters, but on LAMBADA, HellaSwag and PIQA the frozen-table model is better or tied; only ARC-Easy favours the learned table. With a ternary BitNet b1.58 body the whole model is a 46 MB file, still ties the float model on LAMBADA and PIQA, and on a laptop CPU generates 615 to 740 tokens per second in 62 MB of memory, five to six times the speed of the float model's 8-bit GGUF in llama.cpp at a seventh of the memory. The frozen table wins by 1.7 to 2.3 nats on rare words, accepts 10,000 new words after training with a 3% cost where the learned table collapses by 43%, and all of it is released with the weights, the data and every evaluation answer.
authors: Sai Kiran Bathula
bullets: Learned embeddings improve validation loss by 0.20 nats but require 2.6× more trainable parameters.
The frozen-table model is better or tied on LAMBADA, HellaSwag, and PIQA; ARC-Easy favors learned embeddings.
Combined with a ternary BitNet b1.58 body, the model is 46 MB and generates 615–740 tokens/s on a laptop CPU.
The frozen table performs 1.7–2.3 nats better on rare words and supports 10,000 new words with only a 3% cost.
Scope: results target small Gemma-shaped and ternary models, with the table derived from a pretrained embedding via PCA and sign binarization.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces language model memory via frozen embedding table, relevant to memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
papers.tldr: A frozen 16 MB binary vocabulary can replace a large learned embedding table in small and ternary language models with competitive evaluation performance and much lower memory use.

papers.abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.
authors: Hamed Khosravi, Xiaoming Huo
bullets: Targets agents that accept failed checks or stop at weaker conclusions without exploring valid alternatives.
Precommits rules for how each conclusion can be justified before evidence is checked.
A separate program records check outcomes, blocks unsupported conclusions, and guides or performs checks for stronger ones.
On 480 public-record tasks, PRIME eliminated the unjustified conclusions observed in 26.7% of baseline-agent cases.
Its guidance and additional checks improved justified-conclusion scores from 30.1 to 59.2/100; guarantees depend on correct requirements, exact check locations, and sufficient budget.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces PRIME, a framework for verifiable evidence-grounded reasoning in LLM agents using precommitted rules. It focuses on constraint-based verification of agent conclusions.
papers.title: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: PRIME makes LLM-agent decisions verifiable by predefining evidence routes and enforcing conclusions through a programmatic evidence ledger.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon GUI agents rely on visual history to maintain task states, but retaining historical screenshots increases visual-token usage and inference costs, while textual summaries can discard critical state information, undermining long-horizon reliability. We propose ECHOES, which leverages training-time privileged information to guide textual history compression and strengthen long-horizon reasoning. Specifically, ECHOES adopts a Compression-Think-Action (CTA) format to recursively update a textual history state and reason. The same model, given privileged multi-image inputs, serves as a teacher that provides dense token-level on-policy distillation on student-generated CTA rollouts. Our Perception-Memory Fidelity (PMF) Gap-guided OPD-RL framework dynamically balances privileged distillation and task-reward optimization, with periodic teacher updates supporting continued improvement. We further introduce ECHOESBMK, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark derived from real GUI agent failure trajectories to jointly evaluate visual perception and cross-modal state retention. Experiments on four GUI benchmarks and ECHOESBMK demonstrate substantial gains in task performance and memory fidelity. Without retaining historical screenshots at deployment, ECHOES achieves competitive performance with a favorable performance-inference-cost trade-off and exhibits positive zero-shot transfer to unseen visual planning tasks.
authors: Tengda Guo (Tsinghua University), Jiawang Hu (StepFun), Yifei Tao (Nanyang Technological University), Yin Wang (StepFun), Haotian Hu (Zhejiang Leapmotor Technology Co., Ltd), Fanyi Wang (Honor), Liujuan Tang (StepFun)
bullets: Addresses the tension between retaining costly historical screenshots and losing critical information through textual summaries.
Uses a recursive Compression-Think-Action format to update textual history and guide reasoning.
Applies privileged multi-image teacher guidance through token-level on-policy distillation, balanced with task rewards by PMF Gap-guided OPD-RL.
Introduces ECHOESBMK, a diagnostic benchmark for visual perception and cross-modal state retention based on GUI failure trajectories.
Shows gains across four GUI benchmarks and ECHOESBMK, with favorable performance–inference-cost trade-offs and zero-shot transfer to unseen visual planning tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes recursive textual history compression and memory-fidelity distillation for GUI agents, fitting persistent agent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: ECHOES: Seeing Beyond the Current Image via Recursive History Compression and Privileged On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: ECHOES enables long-horizon GUI agents to compress visual history into text while preserving task-relevant state, reducing inference costs without retaining screenshots at deployment.

papers.abstract: LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.
authors: Mowafak Allaham, Aditya Vempaty, Ashish Jagmohan, Prasenjit Dey, Ravi Kokku
bullets: Underspecified task descriptions can omit verifier-relevant edge cases, motivating clarification before formalization.
An elicitation agent decomposes tasks, asks up to 3 or 10 bounded questions to a reference-grounded simulated developer, and refines the natural-language specification before Lean translation.
Across 189 Verina Lean 4 tasks, same-model elicitation reduced strict pass@1 estimates, while several cross-model pipelines improved them.
The largest reported strict improvement was +6.3 percentage points in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline; effects also varied between basic and advanced tasks.
Postconditions were the main source of degradation, indicating that clarified specifications must be translated reliably into Lean.
papers.selection_reason: Studies an elicitation agent that uses clarification questions to improve the quality of Lean specifications generated by LLMs. This explores interactive prompting and agent-based formalization.
papers.title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
papers.tldr: Interactive clarification can improve Lean specification generation in some cross-model setups, but its benefits are inconsistent and depend on the models, question budget, and task type.

papers.abstract: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter-updating test-time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation-valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot-matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre-relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never-seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning-savings
authors: Zhe Zhou
bullets: Tests whether later relearning reflects the specific fact previously learned, rather than familiarity with its components or query format.
Compares matched histories: correct binding (LEARNED), exposure without the binding (CONTROL), and a competing answer in the same slot (WRONG).
In Qwen2.5-1.5B, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL after rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning and partial forgetting.
WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, supporting binding-specific savings, though competitor interference may affect this comparison.
A secondary descriptive analysis estimates roughly 18% fewer optimizer updates for restoration after prior learning, using an unpaired never-seen pool.
papers.selection_reason: Relearning savings in test-time continual learning for language models fits adaptation and memory.
papers.title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning
papers.tldr: Prior learning of a specific fact leaves a measurable relearning advantage even after partial forgetting, indicating that current accuracy can underestimate retained knowledge.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems communicate in text, which is lossy and wasteful: the sender throws away the reading it already did. A growing literature instead transmits the KV cache, the natural carrier of that reading. We study the most appealing form of the idea: both models stay frozen and the sender's cache is substituted for the reader's with nothing trained. It does not work, and the obstruction belongs to the reader. A frozen transformer reads only caches close to the one it would have written itself, a region we call its tolerable set. We show that geometric similarity to that cache does not predict whether the reader can use it, and the failure is not gradual, so a more faithful substitute is not the remedy it appears to be. We explain this phenomenon with competitive attention. Experimentally, we test eight diverse substitution methods against two measured anchors: an uninformative cache baseline and the reader's own accuracy from having read the passage. All sit at the baseline. That turns a long tail of separate negative results into one outcome with a stated condition for overturning it. A different design does work: if the reader keeps its own cache and attends over the sender's as extra context, adapting only its queries, it beats its own baseline, and also clears the baseline with eight senders pooled where undirected attention over the same union falls below it. We offer this as a characterization on one probe, not a leaderboard claim. Our central contribution is a redirection: pursuing faithful substitute caches is the wrong target; adding a cache to what the reader already has is the promising one.
authors: Adam Deng
Shicheng Liu
Yada Zhu
bullets: The study examines training-free KV-cache substitution between frozen LLMs as a less lossy alternative to text communication.
Readers only tolerate caches near those they would have produced themselves, but geometric similarity does not predict usability and failure is abrupt rather than gradual.
Competitive attention is offered as an explanation for why more faithful cache substitutes do not solve the problem.
Eight substitution methods perform at the uninformative-cache baseline, while a query-adaptation design that preserves the reader’s cache exceeds its own baseline in the reported probe.
The authors characterize this as a redirection from replacing reader caches to augmenting them with sender caches, not as a broad leaderboard claim.
papers.selection_reason: Studies KV cache substitution and cache-augmented inference in LLM systems, directly relevant to KV cache and memory efficiency.
papers.title: Close Enough is Nowhere Near: Fidelity-Consumability Decoupling in KV Caches
papers.tldr: Frozen readers cannot reliably use substituted sender KV caches, even when those caches are geometrically similar; retaining the reader’s cache and adding the sender’s as context is more promising.

papers.abstract: Tiny robots have limited computation and memory, yet visual navigation systems often maintain more state than a task requires. We ask whether persistent memory can instead be shaped by the task. We present \textbf{RingNav}, a \(10.6\)k--parameter visual heading estimator that constrains its memory to the circular manifold \(S^1\). RingNav learns only the turn between consecutive images, while heading is composed directly on the circle. On the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge, RingNav reduces mean absolute turn error by \(27\%\) and accumulated heading error over $4$ sec by \(15\%\) relative to a similarly sized learned-memory model. The structured update also gives exactly zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal. Without fine-tuning, RingNav transfers to real-world drone experiments and continues estimating heading under severe visual degradation. RingNav runs at $27.3$Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and can be deployed on an ultra-low power GAP8 processor at $33.4$Hz.
authors: Naitri Rajyaguru
Aryan Tajne
Stephen Jardim
Cornelia Fermuller
Yiannis Aloimonos
bullets: Addresses the excessive state maintained by visual navigation systems on computation- and memory-constrained robots.
Uses a 10.6k-parameter model that predicts only the turn between consecutive images and composes heading directly on the circle S¹.
Reduces mean absolute turn error by 27% and 4-second accumulated heading error by 15% versus a similarly sized learned-memory model on the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge.
Provides exact zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal.
Transfers without fine-tuning to real-world drone experiments and runs at 27.3 Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and 33.4 Hz on GAP8.
papers.selection_reason: Learned visual heading estimator for tiny robots with task-shaped circular memory; relevant to robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: RingNav: Task-Shaped Circular Memory for Visual Heading
papers.tldr: RingNav is a tiny visual heading estimator whose memory is constrained to the circular manifold, enabling efficient and robust navigation on resource-limited robots.

papers.abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
authors: Andrea Yaoyun Cui
Hanyu Wang
Xinyi Wang
Bangzheng Li
Lin Zhang
Zhenggang Tang
Shyamal Buch
Dejia Xu
Matthew Tancik
bullets: Benchmarks robustness to 11 hardware/setup perturbation axes across four LIBERO suites, with five severity levels and 210 conditions.
Evaluates nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and statistical testing.
Pooled success decreases from 0.932 under nominal conditions to 0.767 at medium severity and 0.509 at the highest severity.
Robustness varies substantially by perturbation axis and action interface.
Training on visual perturbations does not address faults that do not alter camera images; fixed-parameter episode manifests are released.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for vision-language-action robot policies under hardware perturbations, directly fitting VLA and robot learning/manipulation.
papers.title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: LIBERO-RIG shows that vision-language-action policies can degrade sharply under realistic robot hardware and setup changes, even when task visuals remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video provides a continuous first-person record of everyday activities, making it a natural foundation for wearable AI assistants. Unlike offline video understanding, streaming systems must process observations as they arrive, while queries may refer to experiences from the distant past. Recent work has begun to explore whether information can be recalled across long temporal gaps. Yet remembering how far is only part of the challenge: recurring objects, actions, and locations also require models to remember exactly which detail belongs to which event. We introduce EgoProbe, a benchmark that evaluates streaming egocentric memory along these two complementary dimensions: long-range retention, i.e., how far, and event-specific recall under interference, i.e., how exact. Built on long-form egocentric videos, EgoProbe uses an event-grounded data engine to extend recall intervals, identify related events, and construct event-grounded distractors, followed by human verification. It contains two subsets: EgoProbe-Base, which evaluates long-range recall without intervening related events, and EgoProbe-Echo, which challenges models with similar intervening events and event-grounded distractors. EgoProbe-Echo adopts coarse-to-fine multi-turn probing: the first turn evaluates coarse-grained event recall, while the second tests whether the model can retrieve the target-specific detail associated with the designated event. Extensive evaluation across diverse models reveals substantial limitations in long-range recall, with further challenges in recovering target-event details among related experiences. Even when models correctly answer coarse-grained questions, they often fail to recall the specific details of the designated event. EgoProbe exposes this underexplored failure mode and provides a testbed for advancing long-range and exact memory in streaming egocentric video understanding.
authors: Haokai Pang
Yuqian Fu
Yifei Wang
Yujiao Shen
Tianwen Qian
Mohamed Elhoseiny
Hongbo Fu
bullets: Evaluates two dimensions of memory: long-range retention and event-specific recall under interference.
Introduces EgoProbe-Base for unobstructed long-range recall and EgoProbe-Echo for recall amid similar events and distractors.
Uses an event-grounded data engine with human verification to construct extended recall intervals and targeted probes.
EgoProbe-Echo uses coarse-to-fine multi-turn questions to test event identification followed by target-detail retrieval.
Models show substantial weaknesses, often answering coarse event questions correctly while missing details from the designated event.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for long-range and exact memory in streaming egocentric video.
papers.title: EgoProbe: Benchmarking Long-Range and Exact Memory in Streaming Egocentric Videos
papers.tldr: EgoProbe benchmarks whether streaming video models can both remember distant egocentric events and retrieve the exact details tied to the correct event.

papers.abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) have recently shown that a single humanoid policy can support diverse whole-body control, but extending such generality to physical interaction remains challenging. We introduce I-BFM, to our knowledge the first BFM for humanoid-object interaction. Rather than relying on task-specific policies or reference tracking, I-BFM learns a shared representation of the coupled dynamics among the humanoid, objects, and their contacts using forward-backward representations and unsupervised reinforcement learning. Given a downstream task reward, the same policy can be directly conditioned on a latent command to execute closed-loop interaction without task-specific policy optimization. To improve interaction control over different time scales, we further train the policy with both short-horizon interaction targets and longer-horizon goal targets. A single I-BFM policy performs carrying, pushing, and kicking, while also supporting goal reaching, motion tracking, stylistic control, and long-horizon task chaining. More importantly, it remains effective after large deviations from nominal execution: on Carry, I-BFM achieves 94.3% nominal success and retains 89.3% success after robot falls, compared with 1.3% for a planning-based baseline. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 further demonstrate diverse loco-manipulation behaviors, rapid recovery from interaction failures and external disturbances, and task chaining without task-specific retraining.
authors: Ziqi Han
Yitang Li
Junhan Sun
Fanrong Dong
Yaojie Shen
Lei Ye
Zetong Jing
Yongqi Zhang
Yiming Zhang
Xue Wang
Hao Zhao
bullets: Learns shared representations of coupled humanoid–object–contact dynamics using forward-backward representations and unsupervised reinforcement learning.
Conditions one policy on downstream task rewards through latent commands for closed-loop interaction.
Combines short-horizon interaction targets with long-horizon goal targets to support multiple control time scales.
Supports carrying, pushing, kicking, goal reaching, motion and stylistic control, and long-horizon task chaining.
On Carry, achieves 94.3% nominal success and 89.3% after robot falls; real-world tests on a Unitree G1 show recovery from failures and disturbances.
papers.selection_reason: Humanoid-object interaction policy via unsupervised RL.
papers.title: I-BFM: Reward-Conditioned Robust Humanoid Interaction via Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: I-BFM is an unsupervised, reward-conditioned humanoid foundation model that enables robust, reusable whole-body object interaction without task-specific policy retraining.

papers.abstract: Recent works augment Vision-Language Models with geometry features from pretrained 3D models, expecting that the geometric signal will boost spatial reasoning. However, we find that simply fusing geometry features and training on standard spatial QA yields only marginal improvements on high-level multi-hop tasks. We attribute this gap to a training-signal problem: standard spatial QA can be largely answered from visual features and language priors, so the geometry pathway receives weak gradients and fails to integrate with the visual features. To provide a training signal that requires geometry, we propose \textbf{novel-view semantic rendering} as an auxiliary training task that requires the model to predict the semantic layout of an unobserved viewpoint, inspired by humans' ability to mentally simulate novel viewpoints during spatial reasoning. This task encourages joint use of both pathways: geometry provides pose-dependent visibility, while vision provides semantic content. Our auxiliary task yields consistent improvements over the geometry-augmented baseline across all three benchmarks (up to +1.6 on VSI-Bench, +2.2 on ReVSI, +2.9 on our 3D-Point-QA dataset) and our full model surpasses prior open-source methods on VSI-Bench and on ReVSI. Project page: https://yuqunw.github.io/Render2Reason/.
authors: Yuqun Wu
Yao Xiao
Chuhang Zou
Shenlong Wang
Derek Hoiem
bullets: Simply adding pretrained 3D geometry features provides limited gains because standard spatial QA can rely on vision and language priors.
The proposed auxiliary task predicts the semantic layout from an unobserved viewpoint, requiring mental-style spatial simulation.
Geometry supplies pose-dependent visibility while visual features provide semantic content, encouraging pathway integration.
The method improves over the geometry-augmented baseline by up to 1.6 on VSI-Bench, 2.2 on ReVSI, and 2.9 on 3D-Point-QA.
It surpasses prior open-source methods on VSI-Bench and ReVSI.
papers.selection_reason: Improves spatial understanding in VLMs via novel-view semantic rendering.
papers.title: Render to Reason: Novel-View Semantic Prediction Improves Spatial Understanding in VLMs
papers.tldr: Novel-view semantic rendering gives geometry-augmented VLMs a stronger training signal, improving spatial reasoning across three benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables robot policies to improve through physical interaction, but the assistance they require changes as their competence evolves. Existing intervention strategies based on offline estimates or fixed decision rules can therefore become mismatched to the current policy. To address this, we propose UniIntervene++, an adaptive intervention agent that learns to allocate control between autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors during online RL. Specifically, UniIntervene++ first formulates the evolving RL policy, trajectory correction, and a task-structured CodePolicy as Options in a unified semi-Markov decision process and learns their relative values online. Building on this, competence-adaptive intervention periodically probes the RL policy through unassisted execution, keeping control allocation responsive to its evolving capability. Finally, coupled experience learning allows assisted behaviors to improve the RL policy, whose evolving outcomes in turn reshape future intervention decisions. In this way, UniIntervene++ jointly determines when to intervene, how to intervene, and when to return control as the RL policy improves. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, UniIntervene++ achieves an average success rate of 89.67%, outperforming all baselines by at least 6 percentage points, while reducing human intervention to 0.77%, a relative reduction of at least 94.6% from the best baseline. Code is available in our \href{https://github.com/dannyyudong/An-Adaptive-Intervention-Agent-for-Efficient-Real-World-Reinforcement-Learning}{GitHub repository}.
authors: Yudong Lin
Haoyuan Deng
Zhuoxuan Yuan
Zaijia Yang
Yuanjiang Xue
Ziwei Wang
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed or offline intervention rules and an RL policy whose competence changes during learning.
Models autonomous execution, trajectory correction, and structured CodePolicy assistance as Options in a unified semi-Markov decision process.
Learns option values online and periodically probes unassisted behavior to keep control allocation competence-aware.
Uses coupled experience learning so assisted behaviors improve the RL policy and the policy’s progress updates future intervention choices.
Across five real-world manipulation tasks, reaches 89.67% average success with 0.77% human intervention, outperforming baselines by at least 6 percentage points.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive intervention agent for online RL in real-world robot manipulation, jointly allocating control and reducing human intervention.
papers.title: UniIntervene++: An Adaptive Intervention Agent for Efficient Real-World Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: UniIntervene++ adaptively decides when and how to assist a robot during online reinforcement learning, achieving high task success while sharply reducing human intervention.

papers.abstract: When a large language model solves a mathematical problem, its reasoning is largely hierarchical, and the solution often branches at a few tokens where the next-token entropy is high. Such tree-like structure embeds in hyperbolic space with far lower distortion than in Euclidean space. Activation steering, however, usually edits the hidden states of a pretrained model by adding one fixed Euclidean vector at every token, even though most tokens of a solution are already determined by the context. We propose Hyperbolic Entropy Steering (HEST), which embeds the hidden states in the Poincaré ball with a lightweight probe whose only label is the model's own next-token entropy. Where this entropy exceeds a threshold, HEST moves the embedded state along the geodesic of steepest descent of a readout of the probe and maps the change back to the hidden state. For the Busemann readout of a learned ideal point, we prove that a step of fixed length lowers it by the same amount at every state. On three instruction-tuned models from the Qwen2.5-Math and Llama-3.1 families, HEST with the Busemann readout improves greedy accuracy on MATH-500 and GSM8K in five of six settings, by up to 1.8 points, whereas a contrastive steering vector added at every token lowers accuracy. With a Euclidean probe trained in the same way, this gain disappears on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct. The gains are largest on problems where the model hesitates often, and accuracy on the remaining problems is almost unchanged.
authors: Zeyong Zhang
Tung Sum Thomas Kwok
Tengfei Ma
Mengjia Xu
bullets: Motivation: Mathematical reasoning is hierarchical and branches mainly at tokens with high next-token entropy, while standard steering applies the same Euclidean edit everywhere.
Method: A lightweight probe maps hidden states into the Poincaré ball using the model’s own entropy; above a threshold, it applies geodesic descent and maps the update back.
Theory: With a Busemann readout, a fixed-length hyperbolic step lowers the readout by the same amount at every state.
Results: Across three Qwen2.5-Math and Llama-3.1 models, HEST improves greedy accuracy on MATH-500 and GSM8K in five of six settings, by up to 1.8 points.
Scope: Gains are largest on problems with frequent hesitation, while other problems remain nearly unchanged; the gain disappears with a matched Euclidean probe on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct.
papers.selection_reason: Entropy-trained hyperbolic probes for sparse activation steering in instruction-tuned LLMs improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.title: Hesitation Has a Geometry: Entropy-Trained Hyperbolic Probes for Sparse Activation Steering
papers.tldr: HEST steers mathematical reasoning only at high-entropy decision points, using hyperbolic geometry to improve greedy accuracy without disrupting confident tokens.

papers.abstract: Visually plausible articulated assets may still fail during contact interactions or exhibit inaccurate motion. We present FACT (Fidelity-Aware Construction of Articulated Twins), an agentic framework that progressively constructs articulated twins to improve geometry, contact, and dynamic fidelity. The agent drives an evidence--diagnosis--revision loop on a shared editable representation, selecting measurements and model edits using quantitative feedback, while numerical tools execute and validate the updates. It reconstructs editable articulated geometry from images through feature planning, targeted measurements, and diagnostic refinement. On this reference, it repairs collision proxies through task-aware local repartitioning before fidelity-constrained compression. Finally, it constructs response models from passive-response videos, using simulation residuals to guide model revision and constrained physical parameter fitting. Experiments show that FACT improves geometric reconstruction over baselines, enables more reliable interaction with simpler collision proxies, and better reproduces held-out physical responses than direct parameter inference.
authors: Kuixiang Shao
Chuansen Nie
Yinuo Bai
Jiayuan Gu
Jingyi Yu
bullets: Targets failures in visually plausible assets, including inaccurate motion and unreliable contact interactions.
Uses an evidence–diagnosis–revision loop on a shared editable representation, guided by quantitative feedback and numerical validation.
Reconstructs editable articulated geometry from images through feature planning, targeted measurements, and diagnostic refinement.
Repairs collision proxies with task-aware local repartitioning, then applies fidelity-constrained compression.

Learns response models from passive-response videos using simulation residuals and constrained physical parameter fitting; experiments report better reconstruction, interaction reliability, and held-out response reproduction than direct inference.
papers.selection_reason: Agentic construction of articulated 3D twins from images and videos, improving geometry, contact, and dynamic fidelity.
papers.title: FACT: Fidelity-Aware Construction of Articulated Twins
papers.tldr: FACT is an agentic framework that iteratively builds articulated twins with improved geometry, contact behavior, and physical response fidelity.

papers.abstract: Pretrained robot policies offer strong manipulation skills but are typically limited to single-agent settings, where a robot acts in isolation. In this work, we study how to adapt pretrained single-agent diffusion policies to multi-agent settings using minimal collaborative data, co-optimizing for two key objectives: high coordination performance and single-agent skill retention. To this end, we introduce ALTER, an adaptation method for coordination on demand: the adapted policy coordinates with other robots when deployed in a team while remaining capable of acting independently when operating alone. Execution is decentralized: each robot acts only on its own visual observations, without explicit inter-agent communication. Our method trains a coordination head that predicts a residual denoiser to transform single-agent behavior into coordinated multi-agent behavior when necessary while also preserving single-agent capabilities. To preserve single-agent capabilities, we augment a small number of collaborative demonstrations with self-distilled data generated by the base policy during training of the residual denoiser. In simulation, ALTER achieves higher coordination success over our baselines while retaining much higher source-skill retention. In our hardware experiments, we find similar trends where ALTER better co-optimizes for coordination success and single-agent skill retention than the baselines.
authors: Dayi Dong
Maulik Bhatt
Aayushi Shrivastava
Lasse Peters
Negar Mehr
bullets: Targets on-demand coordination: robots collaborate in teams but act independently when alone.
Trains a coordination head that predicts a residual denoiser to modify single-agent behavior when needed.
Uses self-distilled data from the base policy alongside a small number of collaborative demonstrations to retain source skills.
In simulation and hardware experiments, ALTER improves the coordination–skill-retention trade-off over baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts pretrained single-agent diffusion policies to multi-agent manipulation while preserving single-agent skills via residual denoising.
papers.title: Residual Denoising Enables Sample-Efficient Multi-Agent Coordination on Demand
papers.tldr: ALTER adapts pretrained single-agent diffusion policies for decentralized multi-robot coordination using minimal collaborative data while preserving independent operation.

papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into executable SQL queries, but open-source large language models still require task-specific post-training for complex, real-world SQL generation. Effective post-training requires both training data that cover the capabilities demanded by the target task and a learning strategy that enables the model to acquire them. Existing datasets provide valuable supervision but incompletely cover SQL structures, while augmentation methods typically expand data without identifying structural gaps. Moreover, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning (RL) alone cannot dynamically address weaknesses exposed during training. We propose COAL-SQL, a unified framework combining Coverage-Guided Augmentation (CGA) and Failure-Driven Learning (FDL). CGA uses greedy selection to identify SQL structures missing from the original dataset and constructs complementary examples, improving structural coverage. FDL retains GRPO as the main optimization objective while supplying targeted supervision for unsolved examples. At the step level, it applies SFT to verified reasoning traces generated by a strong LLM for accumulated failures. At the epoch level, it retrieves structurally related examples based on accumulated failures to create targeted practice, helping the model acquire the corresponding SQL capabilities. With only 12,600 distinct post-training examples, COAL-SQL achieves 64.9% execution accuracy on the BIRD development set and outperforms baselines trained at comparable scale. The code is available at https://github.com/TechNomad-ds/COAL-SQL.
authors: Qifeng Cai
Xuanguang Pan
Hao Liang
Chang Xu
Wentao Zhang
bullets: Addresses incomplete SQL-structure coverage and static training strategies in existing post-training data and methods.
Uses Coverage-Guided Augmentation to greedily identify missing structures and generate complementary examples.
Uses Failure-Driven Learning with GRPO, step-level SFT on verified reasoning traces, and epoch-level retrieval of structurally related practice examples.
With 12,600 post-training examples, reaches 64.9% execution accuracy on the BIRD development set and outperforms comparably scaled baselines.
Scope: focuses on complex, real-world Text-to-SQL generation for open-source language models.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training framework for open-source LLMs on text-to-SQL with coverage-guided augmentation and failure-driven learning.
papers.title: COAL-SQL: Coverage-Guided Augmentation and Failure-Driven Learning for Text-to-SQL Post-Training
papers.tldr: COAL-SQL improves Text-to-SQL post-training by filling SQL-structure coverage gaps and targeting examples the model repeatedly fails to solve.

papers.abstract: Can gradient-based training learn the rank needed to store and compose associations in a matrix memory? In our earlier study, we used a matrix-augmented reasoner on a task that admits a rank-1 solution, leaving this question open. We train matrix memories on $K$ fresh key-value bindings whose exact linear recovery requires $\mathrm{rank}(Z) \geq K$. A fixed linear readout queries a single matrix state without access to the original bindings. Experiments measure recovery by cosine similarity greater than 0.9, a threshold distinct from mathematical equality. Learned effective rank increases with $K$ across the tested grid (Spearman $ρ= 1.0$ at $d = 16$). Training-time rank caps produce a recovery transition near $k = K$: at $d = 8$, $K = 4$, rank 3 gives at most 0.0004 recovery and rank 4 gives 0.97. Four of five seeds retain at least 0.9996 recovery through 21-fold self-application of the trained operator. On the entity subspace, the learned operator has effective rank close to $K$ and approximates the ideal cycle. For the single converged seed capped below $K$, a calculation using the entity-subspace operator and ideal cycle predicts the measured cosine within 0.008 through seven applications. Extending training resolves several initial failures, but recovery still declines at larger matrix dimensions with encoder width fixed.
authors: Samuel Larson
bullets: The task stores K fresh key–value bindings whose exact linear recovery requires rank at least K.
Learned effective rank increases with K across the tested settings, with Spearman ρ = 1.0 at d = 16.
Rank below K sharply limits recovery, while rank K enables high recovery in the reported d = 8, K = 4 case.
Most seeds preserve at least 0.9996 recovery through 21 self-applications of the learned operator.
Recovery can decline at larger matrix dimensions when encoder width remains fixed; cosine recovery is an empirical threshold, not exact equality.
papers.selection_reason: Trained matrix memories as associative key-value storage are transferable to persistent/external memory mechanisms for language models.
papers.title: When the Gradient Sees Rank: Provable Necessity, Causal Recruitment, and Composition in Trained Matrix Memories
papers.tldr: Gradient-based training learns matrix-memory rank that scales with the number of associations, enabling near-exact recovery and repeated composition when rank is sufficient.

papers.abstract: This study asks whether training-time motion-prior regularization can improve insertion success when a diffusion policy is learned from only 15 demonstrations. Minimum jerk discourages abrupt changes in predicted translational acceleration; speed-curvature regularization instead couples movement speed to path geometry. These are candidate mechanisms for task completion, not safety guarantees. We compare the priors individually and jointly, neither prior, and generic smoothness, with 80 real-robot trials per setting pooled over four recorded condition classes. Joint and minimum-jerk-only settings each achieved 70/80 successes (87.5%), versus 69/80 (86.3%) for speed-curvature only, 66/80 (82.5%) for neither prior, and 67/80 (83.8%) for generic smoothness. Success rates and Wilson 95% confidence intervals are visualized for direct comparison. Joint regularization exceeded neither by 5.0 percentage points but provided no observed gain over minimum jerk alone. The results motivate minimum jerk as the simpler candidate for replication, without establishing synergy, biomechanical specificity, improved safety, or distribution-shift robustness.
authors: Ning Hu
Shuai Li
Jindong Tan
bullets: Evaluates motion-prior regularization for diffusion-policy robotic insertion under data scarcity.
Compares minimum jerk, speed-curvature, their combination, no prior, and generic smoothness.
Uses 80 real-robot trials per setting across four recorded condition classes.
Minimum jerk and joint regularization each achieved 70/80 successes (87.5%); no prior achieved 66/80 (82.5%).
Findings support minimum jerk as the simpler replication candidate, with limited scope for safety or distribution-shift claims.
papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of motion-prior regularization for diffusion-policy robotic insertion fits robot manipulation and imitation learning.
papers.title: Dissecting Motion-Prior Regularization for Data-Scarce Robotic Insertion
papers.tldr: With only 15 demonstrations, minimum-jerk regularization matched joint regularization and produced the highest observed insertion success, but no synergy or safety benefit was established.

papers.abstract: Robot swarms, by virtue of their decentralised architecture, are a natural tool for scalable, robust modelling of spatial fields, such as water temperature, wind velocity, or terrain elevation. However, existing methods rely on external positioning systems that allow each robot to determine its own position in space. Here, we introduce location-unaware Gaussian process regression (LU-GPR) as a solution to the modelling of spatial fields in the absence of such positioning systems. LU-GPR allows each robot to infer the posterior mean and variance of the field in space, while simultaneously agreeing on a common frame of reference with its peers, using only local sensing and communication. We propose an online algorithm that allows each robot to consistently infer local estimates as its local frame of reference converges to the common one. By means of a product of experts model, each robot also combines the estimates of its peers with its own to obtain a global model. Our results show that LU-GPR scales well with the number of robots and is robust to limited communication ranges. We also demonstrate how it can be used in real-world monitoring scenarios to estimate the flow of an evacuating crowd.
authors: Guillermo Legarda Herranz
Gianpiero Francesca
Mauro Birattari
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable spatial-field modelling when robots cannot determine their absolute positions.
Each robot jointly estimates field posterior mean and variance while aligning its local reference frame with peers.
An online algorithm supports consistent local estimates as frames converge to a shared reference.
A product-of-experts model fuses local and peer estimates into a global field model.
The approach scales with swarm size, tolerates limited communication ranges, and is demonstrated for monitoring an evacuating crowd’s flow.
papers.selection_reason: Decentralized robot-swarm spatial field modeling with common-frame agreement is a meaningful embodied multi-agent perception and reasoning contribution.
papers.title: Gaussian Processes for Modelling Spatial Fields with Robot Swarms
papers.tldr: LU-GPR enables robot swarms to collaboratively model spatial fields without external positioning systems, using only local sensing and communication.

papers.abstract: An agent that learns from rewards has to trust whatever reports those rewards. When the reports suddenly change, either the world changed or the reporter broke. From the reports alone these are indistinguishable, and reinforcement learning theory shows that no amount of further experience separates them. The prescribed escape is richer data about the reporter itself. We ask whether a frozen language model, handed exactly that data, uses it. We build a two-option game in which a payout swap and a lying reporter produce byte-identical histories. Then we add one verified record: an independent check of one round's real result, printed beside what the reporter said about that round. That single line settles the case. We ask three large models, from two families, to answer one question with one letter. Is the reporter honest or lying? They catch a lying reporter almost perfectly. At the 70B class that holds in every condition we tried; the 32B model slips in one wording. They clear an honest reporter far less often, and how often depends on things that should not matter. Averaged over rounds, letters, and wordings, a 72B model calls an honest reporter a liar 38% of the time when nothing has changed at all, and 58% of the time when the payouts moved. A 70B model from a second family calls an honest reporter a liar 26% and 48% of the time. The failure is not one of reading, because in the situation where nothing changed the same models score 0.96 to 1.00 with the answer printed in the prompt. Which surface feature drives it differs by family. For the Qwen models it is which round the record names, and for Llama it is which letter stands for "honest." Adding the record to a prompt that already states the answer makes Llama less likely to give that answer. We had registered a prediction for that 58% before the run: 35%. The failure is larger than we expected.
authors: Arman Nik Khah
bullets: A payout change and a lying reporter can generate identical reward histories, making them indistinguishable from reports alone.
The study tests whether one verified comparison between the reporter’s claim and the real outcome resolves this ambiguity for language models.
Models nearly always identify lying reporters, but their accuracy for honest reporters varies substantially with wording and other irrelevant surface features.
False accusations are especially frequent when payouts changed, reaching 58% for one 72B-class model and 48% for another 70B-class model.
Providing the verified record alongside an answer can sometimes reduce, rather than improve, the likelihood of selecting that answer.
papers.selection_reason: Uses a large language model to diagnose corrupted reward channels in reinforcement learning agents, relevant to Test-Time Learning and LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Easy to Catch a Liar, Hard to Clear an Honest One: Language Models Diagnosing a Corrupted Reward Channel from a Verified Record
papers.tldr: Large frozen language models reliably detect lying reward reporters but often falsely accuse honest ones, even when given a verified record that resolves the ambiguity.

papers.abstract: Reducing radiation exposure in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is important for patient safety; however, ultra-low-dose imaging suffers from severe noise, which may affect diagnostic interpretation without appropriate image enhancement. While current 3D deep generative models, particularly diffusion models, have shown strong reconstruction fidelity, their practical use can be limited by long inference times. In contrast, faster 2D-based alternatives may have difficulty maintaining volumetric consistency, an important consideration for whole-body PET imaging analysis. To bridge this gap, we propose a one-pass conditional 3D rectified flow (3D Flow) framework for whole-body PET image denoising that incorporates a novel optimized non-uniform sampling strategy. The model is trained with a one-pass linear-interpolant velocity-matching objective. This approach reconstructs a full 3D volume in approximately 30 seconds in our implementation, compared with multi-hour inference for the evaluated 3D DDPM baseline. Evaluations including zero-shot transfer to an independent clinical dataset show that our model achieves favorable global image quality and lesion conspicuity compared with the evaluated 3D DDPM and DDIM baselines, including on challenging short-acquisition data. Furthermore, the proposed method shows promising zero-shot transfer performance across the evaluated datasets and unseen dose levels (down to 1/100 of the standard dose), with artifact-focused visual comparisons supporting the need for further lesion-level validation. By balancing reconstruction fidelity and computational efficiency, this work presents a candidate approach for ultra-low-dose whole-body PET image denoising.
authors: Jiale Shen
Guolin Wang
Chenhao Wang
Xinhui Su
Wei Luo
Feng Yu
bullets: Targets severe noise from ultra-low-dose PET to support safer imaging.
Uses conditional 3D rectified flow with a one-pass velocity-matching objective and optimized non-uniform sampling.
Reconstructs a full 3D volume in approximately 30 seconds in the reported implementation, versus multi-hour inference for the evaluated 3D DDPM.
Shows favorable global quality and lesion conspicuity against evaluated 3D DDPM and DDIM baselines, including short-acquisition data.
Demonstrates promising zero-shot transfer across evaluated datasets and unseen dose levels down to 1/100 of standard dose; lesion-level validation remains needed.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an efficient 3D rectified flow model for PET image denoising, addressing both 3D reconstruction and computational efficiency.
papers.title: Efficient 3D Whole-Body PET Image Denoising via Conditional Rectified Flow With Optimized Sampling Strategy
papers.tldr: A one-pass conditional 3D rectified-flow model enables efficient whole-body PET denoising while preserving volumetric image quality and lesion conspicuity at ultra-low doses.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at programming tasks but frequently fail at deterministic, fine-grained reasoning in natural language, relying heavily on semantic approximations rather than robust symbolic execution. To bridge this gap, we propose MIMIC, a framework that leverages executable code as a rigorous medium for reasoning data synthesis. MIMIC fundamentally transforms algorithms into verifiable reasoning trajectories through narrative fusion, code-guided test synthesis, and dynamic code instrumentation. Crucially, these explicit intermediate execution states naturally form a Code-Instrumented Reward (CIR), providing dense, high-fidelity process supervision for reinforcement learning without external reward models. Extensive evaluations reveal that models trained via SFT and GRPO on our synthesized dataset achieve substantial, consistent gains. Our method significantly elevates accuracy across general reasoning, complex mathematical benchmarks, and fine-grained deterministic tasks, demonstrating that the procedural rigor of executable code can effectively unlock and enhance the generalized reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zjy1298/MIMIC.
authors: Jinyang Zhang
Weibin Liao
Keqin Bao
Sihang Li
Shaobo Wang
Muyang Ye
Hongxin Ding
Yue Fang
Tianyi Tang
Fei Huang
Kexin Yang
Xingzhang Ren
Dayiheng Liu
bullets: Addresses LLMs’ tendency to rely on semantic approximations instead of robust symbolic execution in natural-language reasoning.
Transforms algorithms into reasoning data through narrative fusion, code-guided test synthesis, and dynamic code instrumentation.
Uses intermediate execution states as Code-Instrumented Rewards (CIR) for process supervision without external reward models.
Training with SFT and GRPO yields consistent gains across general reasoning, complex mathematics, and fine-grained deterministic tasks.
The approach is scoped to reasoning learned from executable, algorithmic procedures; the abstract does not specify quantitative results.
papers.selection_reason: Code-centric reasoning data synthesis and process reward for LLM reasoning, fitting LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: The Imitation Game: When LLMs Learn to Reason Like Programs via Code-Centric Reasoning Data Synthesis
papers.tldr: MIMIC uses executable code to synthesize verifiable reasoning trajectories and dense process rewards, improving LLMs’ deterministic and general reasoning abilities.

papers.abstract: When the visual style of text is considered, a wide variety can be observed in font, color, and size. However, when a word is read, its meaning is independent of the style in which it has been written or rendered. In this paper, we investigate whether, and how, the style in which a word is visualized in an image impacts the description that a Large Visual Language Model (LVLM) provides for the concept to which that word refers. Specifically, we investigate how functional text styles (readability-oriented, e.g., black sans-serif) versus decorative styles (display-oriented, e.g., colored cursive/script) affect LVLMs' descriptions of a concept in terms of the attributes of that concept. Our experiments study the situation in which the LVLM is able to correctly identify the concept referred to by a visual text, i.e., by a word or words rendered as an image, and in which the visual text style should not influence the attribute-based description that the LVLM produces. Our experimental results reveal that even when the concept is correctly identified, text style influences the model's attribute-based descriptions of the concept. Our findings demonstrate non-trivial style leakage from text style into semantic inference and motivate style-aware evaluation and mitigation for LVLM-based multimedia systems.
authors: Xiaomeng Wang, Martha Larson, Zhengyu Zhao
bullets: Studies whether font, color, and size affect attribute-based descriptions beyond the word’s meaning.
Compares functional, readability-oriented styles with decorative, display-oriented styles.
Focuses on cases where the LVLM correctly identifies the concept represented by the visual text.
Finds that text style still influences the model’s semantic attribute descriptions.
Motivates style-aware evaluation and mitigation for LVLM-based multimedia systems.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the impact of visual text style on descriptions generated by Large Visual Language Models (LVLMs), revealing style leakage effects. This is an empirical study relevant to LVLM robustness and evaluation.
papers.title: Revealing the Impact of Visual Text Style on Attribute-based Descriptions Produced by Large Visual Language Models
papers.tldr: Even when large visual language models correctly read a word in an image, its visual text style can bias the attributes they describe for the referenced concept.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) inherit their visual and linguistic capabilities from Vision-Language Models (VLMs), yet most VLAs are built from off-the-shelf VLMs that are not adapted to the embodied domain, limiting their downstream performance. In this work, we propose EmbodiedMidtrain to bridge the gap between VLMs and VLAs. We first characterize the data distribution gap between them, showing that VLA data occupy compact regions that are largely separated from the broader VLM distribution, while the degree of alignment varies substantially both across and within VLM data sources. Then, we build a mid-training data engine that leverages a lightweight learnable proximity estimator to select the most VLA-aligned candidates from a large VLM pool, and produce EmbodiedMidtrain-1M, a VLM dataset that we further use to mid-train the VLM before downstream VLA fine-tuning. Experiments on both simulated robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show consistent VLA performance gains over off-the-shelf checkpoints across VLM backbones and VLA action heads. These gains extend to downstream tasks not used to guide data selection. Further analysis reveals that mid-training provides a stronger initialization for VLA fine-tuning, with gains emerging from the earliest steps and widening throughout training. Moreover, the data engine captures both dataset-level and sample-level alignment signals, favoring spatial reasoning over text-centric tasks while preserving the diversity of the VLM data. We will release all code, data and models for future research.
authors: Yiyang Du, Zhanqiu Guo, Haochen Zhang, Annabella Macaluso, Xin Ye, Liu Ren, Yonatan Bisk, Chenyan Xiong
bullets: VLA data occupy compact regions largely separated from broad VLM data, with alignment varying across and within sources.
A lightweight learnable proximity estimator selects VLA-aligned samples from a large VLM pool.
The resulting EmbodiedMidtrain-1M dataset is used for VLM mid-training before downstream VLA fine-tuning.
Improvements appear across VLM backbones, VLA action heads, simulated benchmarks, and real-world tasks, including tasks not used for data selection.
Mid-training yields a stronger initialization, with gains appearing early and increasing during fine-tuning; selection favors spatial reasoning while retaining data diversity.
papers.selection_reason: Mid-training VLMs for VLA models, directly relevant to vision-language-action and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: EmbodiedMidtrain: Bridging the Gap between Vision-Language Models and Vision-Language-Action Models via Mid-training
papers.tldr: EmbodiedMidtrain adapts VLMs to embodied data before VLA fine-tuning, consistently improving robot manipulation performance.
